paper_title: PhyRubric: Rubric-Grounded Diagnostic Evaluation of Physical Commonsense in Text-to-Video Generation

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: As text-to-video (T2V) models are increasingly positioned as world simulators, it is essential to evaluate whether their videos conform to physical commonsense. However, existing benchmarks rely on annotators who rate each video with a single score based on intuition, yielding ratings that are subjective and do not tell which physical principle is violated. We introduce PhyRubric, a rubric-grounded diagnostic framework for evaluating physical commonsense in T2V generation. For each caption, PhyRubric constructs a caption-specific rubric before any video is seen, decomposing the caption into semantic and physical items, and derives scores from item-level verdicts grounded in timestamped evidence. We instantiate this framework as PhyRubric-Bench, which spans 34 categories across five physical domains, and scale it up to PhyRubric-Train with 3,788 videos, on which we fine-tune the open-source PhyRubric-Judge. Empirical results across ten T2V models show that physical commonsense remains far from solved, and that PhyRubric-Judge correlates more closely with human judgments than existing open-source judges while matching the frontier proprietary Gemini 4 Argon. Further analysis provides actionable insights for T2V models.

sections.content: As text-to-video (T2V) models are increasingly positioned as world simulators, it is essential to evaluate whether their videos conform to physical commonsense. However, existing benchmarks rely on annotators who rate each video with single score based on intuition, yielding ratings that are subjective and do not tell which physical principle is violated. We introduce PhyRubric, rubric-grounded diagnostic framework for evaluating physical commonsense in T2V generation. For each caption, PhyRubric constructs caption-specific rubric before any video is seen, decomposing the caption into semantic and physical items, and derives scores from item-level verdicts grounded in timestamped evidence. We instantiate this framework as PhyRubric-Bench, which spans 34 categories across five physical domains, and scale it up to PhyRubric-Train with 3,788 videos, on which we fine-tune the open-source PhyRubric-Judge. Empirical results across ten T2V models show that physical commonsense remains far from solved, and that PhyRubric-Judge correlates more closely with human judgments than existing open-source judges while matching the frontier proprietary Gemini 4 Argon. Further analysis provides actionable insights for T2V models. 1. Introduction Text-to-video (T2V) generation has advanced rapidly, and recent T2V models [1, 13, 45, 57, 59, 62, 67] can now render complex scenes from text prompts. As these models are increasingly positioned as world simulators [1, 33, 68], basic requirement is that their videos conform to physical commonsense, the shared expectations about the physical world that everyone acquires from everyday experience, without any textbook physics [37, 55]. reliable and comprehensive evaluation of this ability is therefore essential for tracking progress and guiding model development. Figure 1. Intuition-based rating vs. rubric-grounded evaluation. (a) Two raters give different scores to the same video, and the scores alone do not say what went wrong. (b) Checking the video against caption-specific rubric item by item yields scores with the violated expectation and its timestamp. Existing benchmarks for physical commonsense have made notable progress [7, 8, 19, 47], but they share two limitations  (Fig. 1)  . First, the ratings are subjective. Annotators rate each video and its caption with single score on discrete scale, but no rule defines how physical violations map to scores. Each rater thus applies an intuitive mapping, weighing the severity of violations by personal standards, so the same video may receive different scores. This inconsistency introduces noise into both benchmark results and the automatic evaluators trained on these ratings. Second, the ratings are uninterpretable. discrete scale is easier to rate than continuous one, since fractional scores would be harder to assign and more scattered. However, single score reflects only how implausible video is overall, not which physical principle is violated. Evaluations can thus only rank models and categories, yielding coarse findings that offer little guidance for improvement. To address these limitations, we introduce PhyRubric, rubric-grounded diagnostic framework for evaluating physi1 cal commonsense in T2V generation  (Fig. 2)  . For each caption, PhyRubric constructs caption-specific rubric before any video is seen, and reuses it for every video generated from that caption. The rubric decomposes the caption into verifiable items of two types: semantic items list the visible facts the caption requires, while physical items specify which visible events count as violations and are each assigned severity level inspired by the order in which infants acquire physical knowledge [6, 41, 55]. Given video, each item receives verdict grounded in timestamped evidence, and scores are derived deterministically from these verdicts rather than rated directly. Every score thus comes with diagnosis of which expectation failed and why. We instantiate this framework as PhyRubric-Bench. Unlike prior benchmarks dominated by mechanics (Suppl. Tab. 4), it spans 34 categories across five physical domains: mechanics, optics, heat, electricity, and acoustics1. Every caption describes complete causal event and states its outcome explicitly, so that semantic adherence requires rendering the cause, the action, and its physical consequence, e.g., the key switch is turned, and the lamp lights rather than the key switch is turned. Beyond PhyRubric-Bench, we scale up to PhyRubricTrain, 947 captions that share the taxonomy of the benchmark but no scenes, each paired with its own rubric. Here the rubric plays different role: rather than defining the evaluation as in PhyRubric-Bench, it guides an agentic annotator, telling it which expectations to check and where to look, yielding 3,788 labeled videos from four T2V models with 45.9K rubric-item verdicts. On these labels, we train PhyRubric-Judge, an open-source VLM that needs no rubric at inference. Given only caption and video, it predicts semantic adherence and physical commonsense scores together with diagnosis of which physical expectation is violated and why. We evaluate ten T2V models on PhyRubric-Bench and find that basic physical commonsense remains far from solved: even the strongest model, Seedance 2.5, produces videos that are both faithful to the caption and physically plausible in fewer than half of cases. Moreover, PhyRubricJudge correlates more closely with human judgments than the judges released with existing benchmarks, generalizes well to unseen generators and domains, and provides diagnosis that locates each violation. Our contributions are summarized as follows: We propose PhyRubric, rubric-grounded framework that constructs caption-specific rubric before any video is seen and derives every score from evidence-grounded item verdicts, so that each score comes with diagnosis. We construct PhyRubric-Bench, spanning 34 categories across five physical domains with human-verified rubrics 1Since generated videos are silent, the acoustics domain covers only the visible consequences of sound, such as water rippling beside speaker. and labels, and PhyRubric-Train, labeled by rubricguided agentic annotator, on which we train the opensource PhyRubric-Judge that generalizes to unseen generators and domains. Rather than proposing definitive standard, we show that our rubric-grounded evaluation serves as an analysis tool that yields deeper insights: semantic adherence is the main bottleneck, physical errors are all-or-nothing, and models often avoid physical errors by not depicting the event at all, shortcut that prior protocols reward. 2. Related Work 2.1. Physical Commonsense Benchmarks for Textto-Video Generation The rapid advancement of text-to-video (T2V) generation has motivated range of benchmarks for its assessment [30, 31, 39, 43, 44, 56, 60, 66]. Moving beyond general visual quality, growing line of work focuses on physical commonsense in T2V generation [7, 8, 19, 20, 36, 47, 53], while other works study physical understanding in settings where models are conditioned on observed frames and predict how the scene evolves [33, 40, 48]. However, most of these physical commonsense benchmarks are dominated by mechanics [7, 8, 20], and some include prompts that require specialized knowledge beyond everyday experience [19, 20, 36, 47]. In contrast, PhyRubric-Bench spans five physical domains with prompts grounded in physical commonsense, and pairs each prompt with captionspecific rubric that enables diagnostic evaluation. 2.2. VLM-as-a-Judge for Physical Commonsense Existing evaluation of video generation mainly follows two paradigms: standard metrics such as FVD [58], SSIM [61], and CLIP score [27], and VLM-based evaluation [12, 23, 52] such as VideoScore [25]. As standard metrics cannot capture physical plausibility, physical commonsense evaluation mainly adopts the latter, employing VLMs as dedicated judges. On the open-source side, judges such as VideoCon-Physics [7] and VideoPhy-2-AutoEval [8] are fine-tuned on the human annotations of their corresponding datasets. On the proprietary side, recent works prompt commercial models such as GPT-4o, Gemini-2.5-Pro, and GPT-5.5 as judges [19, 47, 51, 53]. Nevertheless, most of these judges output holistic score rather than detailed diagnosis, failing to reveal what goes wrong and why. 2.3. Rubric-Based Evaluation rubric is an explicit set of criteria that decomposes holistic quality judgment into verifiable items, making the assessment transparent, consistent, and interpretable [14, 32]. Recently, rubrics have been widely adopted for fine-grained evaluation of large language models (LLMs) and vision2 language models [34, 38], and increasingly tailor the criteria to each individual query rather than applying generic rubric to all samples [4, 16, 35]. In text-to-image generation, related line of work decomposes prompts into finegrained questions to assess text-image alignment [15, 29]. However, rubric-based evaluation remains underexplored for physical commonsense in video generation. In this work, rubrics play two roles: they serve as the evaluation criteria of PhyRubric-Bench, and they guide an agentic annotator to label training data for PhyRubric-Judge. 3. PhyRubric As illustrated in Fig. 2, PhyRubric fixes rubric for each caption before any video is seen and shares it across all videos from that caption. This keeps the criteria identical across videos, so that scores from different generators are directly comparable and cannot be swayed by what particular video happens to show. Moreover, rubric reviewed by humans once can be reused for any number of videos, including those from future generators. 3.1. Caption-Specific Rubric Formulation We evaluate generated videos along the two dimensions introduced by VideoPhy-2 [8], semantic adherence (SA) and physical commonsense (PC), each on 15 scale. Unlike prior benchmarks, where annotators assign holistic score to each dimension, we pair every caption with rubric that specifies what video must satisfy to be faithful and physically plausible for that caption. The rubric consists of two groups of items, one for SA and one for PC, and each score is derived from item-level verdicts rather than rated directly. simplified rubric example is shown in Fig. 3. Semantic Adherence (SA). SA measures whether the Its rubric items video shows what the caption describes. are the visible facts the caption requires, in two tiers: Primary: the main objects and each event in the caption. Secondary: the remaining facts, including stated qualifiers (e.g., once, slowly, wooden), initial states implied by the caption, and the order of events. Physical Commonsense (PC). This metric evaluates whether the events shown in the video follow physical commonsense. We define four severity levels for physical violations, inspired by the order in which infants acquire physical knowledge in developmental psychology [6, 41, 55]: Fatal: the scene is impossible as whole, violating core object principles such as permanence, solidity, or continuity (e.g., objects passing through each other, or appearing or vanishing without cause). Core: the central interaction described by the caption does not happen or happens incorrectly (e.g., in reverse or through broken mechanism). Major: clear violation outside the central interaction, such as missing secondary consequence (e.g., the lamp lights but the desk beneath it stays dark). Minor: visual flaw that leaves the event intact, such as color or texture drift of untouched objects. Each PC item is assigned one of these severity levels and one of ten violation types (e.g., permanence, solidity, causeless motion, process direction). Following the same developmental order, the ten types are grouped into L1 core object principles, L2 everyday dynamics, and L3 attribute experience (Suppl. Tab. 6). Each PC item is then judged by pair of verifiable statements: Expect: what physically correct video should show, specifying the moment, region, or event to inspect. Fail: the concrete visible signs that count as violation, and the item fails only if one of these signs is observed. Verdicts. An SA item is judged pass or fail. PC item has third verdict, not shown, which applies when the moment, region, or event specified by its Expect statement never appears in the video. Otherwise, the item fails if any sign in its Fail statement is observed, and passes if not. Note that not shown means the situation is absent, not that the expected behavior failed to occur. For example, for the caption The key switch on the base of desk lamp is turned, and the lamp lights  (Fig. 3)  , if the key is never turned in the video, P2 is not shown rather than failed, since the missing action is already penalized by the SA item S2. Since fail can only be triggered by listed sign, every negative verdict is grounded in specific observation rather than an overall impression, and carries the severity and violation type of its item. Consistent with the nature of commonsense, PC items judge only the direction and order of change rather than its rate or extent, and never penalize cause for being out of view (e.g., heat source or power supply). Scoring Rules. Both scores lie on 15 scale and are derived from the verdicts by fixed rules. For SA, video judged entirely unrelated to the caption scores 1. Otherwise, it scores 5 if all items pass, 4 if only secondary items fail, 3 if exactly one primary item fails, and 2 if two or more primary items fail. Each rubric is checked to contain at least two primary and one secondary SA items and at least one PC item of every severity, so that every score from 1 to 5 is attainable. 3.2. Stating the outcome serves two purposes. (1) Fixed expectations: what should happen is determined before any video is seen, so the rubric can specify the expected events and violations rather than guess among plausible outcomes. The judge thus learns not only what score to give but why (Suppl. Sec. C.3). 3.3. PhyRubric-Train and PhyRubric-Judge Training data annotation. Human verification does not scale to thousands of videos, so we label the training set with the same agentic annotator used to pre-annotate PhyRubric-Bench, built on Claude Sonnet 5.5 [3]. Instead of fixed set of frames, the annotator first scans timestamped overview of the clip and then zooms in at full frame rate where and when it needs to, until each rubric item can be decided from frames that clearly show the relevant event. This matters because physical violations often involve small objects or brief moments that uniform sampling misses. For every item, it returns verdict with timestamped evidence, and the scores follow from the verdicts by the rules in Sec. 3.1. Applied to the 947 training captions, each rendered by four generators, it yields PhyRubric-Train with 3,788 videos and 45.9K item-level verdicts. Suppl. Sec. The agentic annotator produces reliable labels but is impractical as general-purpose evaluator: it relies on proprietary model, makes repeated tool calls per video, and needs rubric for every new caption. We therefore train PhyRubric-Judge, an open-source VLM, on PhyRubricTrain. Starting from Qwen3-VL-8B [5], we explore configurations that vary the rubric input, the output format, and the training objective (SFT or GRPO [54]). Four of them are open-source T2V models that also render PhyRubric-Train: CogVideoX1.55B [64], HunyuanVideo-1.5-8B [62], LTX-Video-2B [21], and Wan2.2-T2V-A14B [59]. All experiments are run on NVIDIA GH200 Superchips. 4.2. Main Results Tab. 1 reports the results of ten video generators on PhyRubric-Bench across five physics domains. We summarize the main findings below. Physical commonsense remains far from solved. The two proprietary models lead by wide margin: Seedance 2.5 achieves an average JP of 44.20% and Veo 3.1 36.20%, two to three times that of the strongest open-source model, HunyuanVideo-1.5-8B (14.93%). Even so, more than half of their videos are still not both faithful to the caption and physically plausible. Moreover, every open-source model has an average SA below 3, indicating that at least one primary element of the caption is typically missing from the generated video. Even among assessable videos, where the intended event does occur, their average PC never exceeds 3.5, suggesting that the event typically violates at least one expectation of major severity or above. Video generative models handle optics best but struggle with heat and acoustics. As shown in Tab. 1, Optics is the strongest domain for eight of the ten evaluated models, and ranks second (or tied for second) for the remaining two models, Seedance 2.5 and CogVideoX1.5-5B. In contrast, Heat and Acoustics are the weakest domains for most models. Even the proprietary models reach only 30.00% (Seedance 2.5) and 15.00% (Veo 3.1) JP on Acoustics, and two open-source models score 0.00% in this domain. We conjecture that optical phenomena (e.g., reflection and shadows) are visually salient and well represented in training data, whereas thermal processes involve gradual state changes and acoustic phenomena must be conveyed through indirect visual cues (e.g., sound-induced ripples on liquid surface), both of which are harder to render. Semantic adherence is the main bottleneck, and physical errors are all-or-nothing. Fig. 5a shows the distribution of SA and PC scores. SA concentrates at 2 (50.8% of all videos), the score given when two or more primary elements of the caption are missing, while only 5.0% of videos receive 4, the score for video that misses only secondary details: most generated videos fail to depict the captioned event itself, before physics even comes into play. In contrast, once the event is fully shown, its physics is usually correct: as shown in Fig. 5b, only 5.9% of videos show the event fully but violate physics (SA4, PC<4), compared with 16.9% that pass, meaning that 74.1% of fully shown events are rendered with plausible physics. Physical errors themselves are all-or-nothing: PC over assessable videos is bimodal, with 52.9% scoring 5, i.e., no violation at all, and 40.8% scoring 1 or 2, i.e., fatal or core violation, whereas scores of 3 and 4, i.e., only major or minor violations, together account for 6.3%. This suggests that when current models do show the event, they either render its physics correctly or break it at the most basic level, and rarely get the core event right but slip on peripheral details. Models take shortcut to high PC by not showing the event. Prior protocols rate PC on every video, so video that never attempts the event leaves nothing for physics to contradict and receives high PC. Conclusion We presented PhyRubric, rubric-grounded framework for diagnostic evaluation of physical commonsense in T2V generation, which fixes caption-specific rubric before any video is seen and derives every score from evidencegrounded item verdicts. Our evaluation of T2V models reveals that physical commonsense remains far from solved, and our in-depth analysis provides actionable insights for developing future T2V models.

sections.title: Supplementary Material
sections.content: A. Dataset and Benchmark A.1. Comparison with Prior Benchmarks Tab. 4 compares PhyRubric with prior benchmarks that evaluate physical commonsense in text-to-video models. Each cell is determined from the benchmarks paper and released code and data, following the criteria below. Domains. Prior benchmarks center on mechanics, such as collisions, falling, and fluid flow. Heat is main category only in PhyGenBench. PhyWorldBench covers heat in two of its 50 subcategories and electricity in one, about 4% and 2% of its prompts, whereas each domain makes up about fifth of PhyRubrics captions. No prior benchmark covers acoustics. These under-covered domains are exactly those in which the cause (e.g., an electric current, heat, or sound) is invisible, so model must link visible trigger to visible effect without seeing what connects them. Commonsense only. We mark this column when every caption can be judged from everyday experience. PhyWorldBench includes an Anti-Physics category whose prompts deliberately violate physics, PhyGenBench organizes its prompts by 27 physical laws, and T2VPhysBench builds its prompts from first-principles laws such as energy conservation. Judging these videos requires treating physical violations as correct or applying formal physics knowledge, neither of which reflects how non-experts judge videos. Rubric. Several benchmarks pair each prompt with questions or standards: PhyGenBench generates physics questions with GPT-4o, PhyWorldBench lists physics standards per prompt, and PhysVidBench derives yes/no questions from each prompt. None of them, however, assigns severity to its items or specifies the visible signs that count as violation, so failed question weighs the same whether an object vanishes or color drifts slightly, and the score is an average of answers rather than rule over severities. PhyRubric fixes both, and every rubric is verified by humans before any video is scored. Train set. Only VideoPhy and VideoPhy-2 release humanlabeled videos for training judge, from which VideoConPhysics and VideoPhy-2-AutoEval are trained. Their labels are holistic 15 ratings, whereas PhyRubric-Train provides item-level verdicts with timestamped evidence. Explainable. judge is explainable when it reports which requirement fails and what in the video supports that verdict. The judges of VideoPhy, VideoPhy-2, and PhyGenBench output scores only. PhyWorldBench and PhysVidBench are partially explainable: each yes/no answer refers Figure 8. Taxonomy of PhyRubric-Bench. The inner circle shows the five physical domains, sized by the number of captions, and the outer ring shows the 34 categories. to one requirement, so negative answer indicates what is missing, but neither cites evidence from the video, and both judges answer from text description of the video rather than from the video itself. Open-source. We mark this column when physicsspecific judge is trained and its weights are released. VideoPhy and VideoPhy-2 release their judges, VideoConPhysics and VideoPhy-2-AutoEval. For each of the 34 categories, Claude Fable 5.1 and GPT-5.6 Sol receive the scope note of the category and the drafting instructions in Sec. E.3, and each model proposes batch of candidates. Beyond the requirements in Sec. 3.2, the instructions add three rules. (1) caption states the trigger and the visible outcome in plain words but never how the outcome unfolds. (2) It contains no law names, numbers, decorative adjectives, or camera directions. (3) Its outcome must hold under every reasonable rendering rather than depend on threshold, such as how hard an object is pushed. Each candidate also comes with two hidden fields that neither the generator nor the VLM judge ever sees: one to three violation types that the event puts at risk, and an expectation briefly describing how the outcome should unfold. Both guide rubric drafting. Candidates are first checked automatically for wellformed record, valid category, and the absence of numerals, and then reviewed manually in two stages. First, the categories are divided between two reviewers. Each reviewer marks every candidate in the assigned categories as keep, edit, or remove, provides revised caption for each edit, and compares the captions within each category for repeated scenes, lack of variety, and events that belong to another domain. The other reviewer then cross-checks every decision and revision. Second, third reviewer goes through all remaining captions to ensure consistent standards across categories. Disagreements are resolved by discussion. Review removed 242 candidates: 99 in heat, 48 in electricity, 48 in mechanics, 24 in acoustics, and 23 in optics. Rubric Construction. E.3. The instructions specify what each item may say: an SA item states fact the caption requires and nothing else, and PC item pairs physical requirement with two to four visible signs of failure, constrains direction and order but never magnitude, and never requires an invisible cause such as heat, current, or sound to be seen. The annotator needs the rubric, whereas the judge takes only the caption (Sec. 3.3). We test this choice in three ways. (1) Giving the judge the rubric as input and training it to output the scores only improves correlation by 0.06 on SA and 0.05 on PC. The rubric thus carries information that the judge cannot fully recover from the caption, but every new caption would then need rubric before the judge can be applied. (2) Giving the rubric and training the judge to output item-wise verdicts instead of scores does not help, as the scores derived from its verdicts are less accurate than directly predicted ones. (3) The rubric is of no use to the untrained model. Given the rubric, zero-shot Qwen3-VL-8B becomes worse on both dimensions, and its PC correlation falls below zero. We therefore keep the caption-only input, so that the judge applies to any new caption, and use the rubric at annotation time only. 9 Where should the diagnosis go? The judge emits the scores first and the diagnosis after them. We compare two alternatives in which the diagnosis is generated first. (1) The diagnosis is the first field of the same JSON object. (2) The diagnosis is chain of thought inside <think> tags, followed by JSON object that holds the scores only. The diagnosis text is identical in all three cases, and only its position changes. Both alternatives lose 0.060.07 on SA and 0.12 on PC. The reason is that the soft score is the expectation over the score tokens (Eq. 2). When the score comes first, this distribution still reflects the uncertainty of the judge. After committed diagnosis, it becomes nearly one-hot, and this uncertainty is lost. Scores first thus keeps an informative soft score and diagnosis. Does reinforcement learning help? Starting from the SFT judge, we continue training the same LoRA with GRPO for one epoch, with 4 samples per prompt at temperature 1, batch of 8 prompts, learning rate of 105, and no KL term. The reward is weighted sum of four terms, = rSA + rPC + 0.5 rfmt + 0.5 rassess, (6) where rfmt rewards valid output format and rassess rewards correct pc assessable flag. The score terms measure how close the predicted score ˆsd is to the label sd: rd = 1 ˆsd sd 4 , {SA, PC}. (7) We run this recipe twice, (1) without thinking, starting from Default, and (2) with thinking, starting from Diagnosis as thinking, and compare each run with its own starting point. As shown in Tab. 14(c), neither run improves over its SFT starting point, and the thinking-free run is clearly better than the one with thinking, especially on PC (r of 0.314 vs. 0.086). possible reason is that GRPO has mainly proven effective on reasoning tasks with verifiable answers, such as mathematics, and may bring less to perceptual task such as judging physical commonsense in video. We leave this to future work and keep SFT as the default. How much training data is needed? PhyRubric-Train is split into 3,600 videos for training and 188 videos from 47 held-out captions for monitoring the training loss. All judges in this paper are trained on the 3,600-video split. We train on random 25% and 50% subsets of it (900 and 1,800 videos) with the same number of epochs  (Fig. 11)  . SA improves only slightly with data (0.58, 0.59, 0.61), whereas PC improves steadily (0.22, 0.25, 0.32). Physical plausibility is thus the dimension that benefits most from more supervision. Qualitative Examples Generated videos. Figs. 1418 show one caption per domain rendered by all ten generators. The two proprietary models render the event in every example, while opensource models most often fail before physics comes into play. Avoidance rarely looks like frozen scene. Instead, the generator skips the action the caption describes: it either shows the outcome from the first frame, as in the fish already hanging from the rod (Cosmos-Predict2.5-14B, Fig. 17) or the phone resting on the pool edge throughout (CogVideoX1.5-5B, Fig. 14), or replaces the action with related one, such as leafing through sheet music (LTX-2.322B, Fig. 18). When the event is shown, the physical errors are brief and local, such as the sheet of paper that emerges from beneath the speaker (Cosmos-Predict2.5-2B, Fig. 18): single rubric item catches it, and the verdict carries the items severity rather than holistic impression. Judge diagnoses. Fig. 19 shows the output of PhyRubricJudge on four videos from PhyRubric-Bench. The diagnosis follows the structure of the training targets: timestamped description of what the video shows, the caption facts that are missing, and each physical violation with the moment it occurs. When the event passes (a), the description is complete timeline of the event. When the event never occurs (b), the judge says so and marks PC as not assessable. When physics breaks (c, d), the judge names the violation and when it occurs, such as fish that tumble with nothing touching them or balls that appear and vanish on the table. all (17.3% of assessable videos) and peaks in acoustics (44.4%) and electricity (24.6%), where an invisible sound or current must produce visible effect, against 9.1% in mechanics. Acoustics also leads in causeless motion (21.8%), since vibration that should follow sound is often rendered as an object that shivers on its own. Process direction concentrates in heat and electricity (11.2% and 13.0%), where melting process reverses or lamp switches back off. Optics carries the appearance types, namely shape and identity (11.7%), where reflection or refracted object does not match its source, and attribute drift (9.3%), where the color of an untouched object changes. Mechanics, where several objects interact, leads in permanence and count (18.5%), material response (8.6%), and trajectory and momentum (8.2%). Each domain thus exposes different class of failure, and benchmark concentrated on mechanics would leave most of these failures unmeasured. Object permanence separates the generators, while missing consequence is shared. Tab. 17 breaks the same rates down by generator, and the two most frequent types behave differently. Permanence and count failures vary by factor of six. Objects appear, vanish, or duplicate in 33.3% of the assessable videos of CogVideoX1.5-5B and in 22 23% of those of LTX-Video-2B and Wan2.2-TI2V-5B, but in only 5.2% for Seedance 2.5 and 8.6% for HunyuanVideo1.5 and Cosmos-Predict2.5-14B, with Veo 3.1 in between at 12.9%. Missing consequence, in contrast, stays between 11% and 22% for every generator, and causeless motion between 6% and 13%. Missing consequence is the most frequent type for all generators except the two weakest, where permanence and count leads. Keeping objects consistent over time thus separates the generators, whereas linking cause to its visible effect is weakness they all share and remains the dominant failure even of the generators that largely keep objects consistent. 12 Figure 14.
